item.title: Would Anthony Volpe's fan-interfered fly ball have been a home run? Here's what MLB and Statcast have to say
item.description: The New York Yankees' ALDS sweep ended with Anthony Volpe's fan-interfered fly ball, and Statcast quietly changed its projected ball flight data.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees' season ended in embarrassing fashion on Wednesday night, getting swept on their home field by their AL East rival Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series.

The Bombers fell, 4-3, to the Rays, but there may be an argument that the game should have been tied at four after Anthony Volpe's fan-interfered fly ball in the sixth inning.

With George Lombard on first and two outs, the Yankees infielder hit a fly ball into left field that kept carrying toward the outfield wall. The ball went into the seats, and umpires initially called it a game-tying home run, but upon replay review, it was turned it into an RBI double instead after an angle clearly showed a fan reach over the wall (he was eventually booted from the ballpark). Spencer Jones struck out to end the threat, and the Yankees would not score again.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"After viewing all relevant angles, the Replay Official definitively determined the spectator interfered with the ball over the field of play. The ball would not have left the playing field nor would it have been caught," MLB's Replay Center said in a statement shortly after the occasion, via the New York Post.

However, MLB's Statcast initially said otherwise.

Volpe hit his ball 357 feet with an exit velocity of 97.9 mph and a 42-degree launch angle. In normal cases, it's an easy flyout, as it had an expected batting average of .060). However, Statcast originally said that the trajectory of the ball would have led to a home run in 13 ballparks, including Yankee Stadium.

But as of Thursday morning, Yankee Stadium is no longer included in stadiums where the ball flight would have been a homer.

Sportsball, perhaps ironically, released a video on X Wednesday morning explaining how Statcast uses 12 Hawkeye cameras in each ballpark to determine home-run distances "within about a foot."

Yankees manager Aaron Boone said the umpires "did a good job" on their call.

"When he hit it, to my eye looking out there, I was a little concerned right away because it felt like something, I wasn't sure. And then seeing the replay and seeing it unfold, I thought they did the right thing. I thought they got it right," Boone said.

"Just seeing it through the replay and hoping for the best. But, crazy," Volpe added.

So, replay shows it very likely would have came up short, Statcast apparently changed its mind, and Major League Baseball says it undoubtedly would have been short.

In any case, it can be argued that no one definitively knows whether Volpe's fly ball would have been gone, and a Yankee fan may or may not have robbed his own favorite team at a chance of a postseason comeback.

item.title: Hillary Clinton issues endorsement in US midterm elections
item.description: Former U.S. Sen. Hillary Clinton endorsed Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan for U.S. Senate as the Democratic candidate runs against Republican Michele Tafoya.
item.content:encoded:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has made her first endorsement of a U.S. Senate candidate in the 2026 midterm elections, backing Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan.

"Minnesota, you have an opportunity to select an extraordinary person and public servant as your next U.S. senator. Please take it!" Clinton wrote in a post on the social media platform Bluesky when sharing a post in which Flanagan touted Clinton's endorsement.

Flanagan declared in her post, "@hillaryclinton.bsky.social has spent five decades fighting for working families, dedicating her career to making the case that every child in this country deserves a fair shot. I’m honored to have Secretary Clinton’s support, and I’ll proudly carry on her fight in the US Senate."

HILLARY CLINTON: 'I HATE' TRUMP AND NETANYAHU'S GOVERNMENTS BUT LOVE AMERICA AND ISRAEL

Clinton, a former first lady and former U.S. senator from New York, was the 2016 Democratic presidential candidate defeated by Republican Donald Trump when he won his first White House contest.

"Donald Trump has made it harder for families to afford childcare, groceries, and health care for their kids. His tariffs and war in Iran are driving up prices, and his budget ripped health care and food assistance away from children so billionaires could get another tax cut," Clinton said in a statement, according to reports.

PEGGY FLANAGAN VOWS TO 'RIP ICE APART' AFTER TOPPLING MODERATE DEM IN KEY SENATE BATTLE

"Peggy Flanagan has spent her career fighting for children and families, from the Children’s Defense Fund to the Lieutenant Governor’s office, and she’s delivered for them," she noted. "I know she’ll be that same champion in the Senate, and I’m proud to endorse her."

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.

Flanagan is facing Republican candidate Michele Tafoya in the Minnesota U.S. Senate contest.

U.S. Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., announced last year that she would not seek re-election in 2026.

item.title: Natalie Wood's daughter confronts very painful way she learned Hollywood icon had died at 11
item.description: Natasha Gregson Wagner describes the childhood sleepover that shattered her world when she learned Natalie Wood had died off Catalina Island.
item.content:encoded:
Natasha Gregson Wagner was just 11 years old when an ordinary childhood sleepover turned into a moment that shattered her world.

While staying at a friend's house, she heard the devastating news on the radio: her mother, Hollywood actress Natalie Wood, was dead.

"As a child, I always knew my mom was home because her Jungle Gardenia scent arrived before she did," Gregson Wagner, now 56, wrote on the website for her fragrance brand, L'Amour Mere. "After she died, I spent hours lying in her bed or sitting in her closet among her clothes. If I could somehow keep her fragrance alive, perhaps she would not be entirely gone."

CHARLIZE THERON RECOUNTS THE NIGHT HER MOTHER FATALLY SHOT HER FATHER WHEN SHE WAS 15 YEARS OLD

In the immediate aftermath of Wood's death, Gregson Wagner said the two father figures in her life — her biological father, British film producer Richard Gregson, and her stepfather, actor Robert Wagner — came together to support her.

"Luckily, I had these two men, Daddy Gregson and Daddy Wagner, who came together and rose to the occasion and completely put me first," Gregson Wagner told the Daily Mail. "They got me into therapy right away, and I had that same amazing therapist here in Beverly Hills until my 20s."

Wood, who was nominated for three Oscars and starred in "West Side Story" and "Rebel Without a Cause," was on the family's yacht with Wagner, actor Christopher Walken and captain Dennis Davern during Thanksgiving weekend in 1981. Her body was found floating in the water off Southern California's Catalina Island. She was 43.

WATCH: ROBERT WAGNER'S MOST MEMORABLE ROLES, FROM ‘HART TO HART’ TO ‘AUSTIN POWERS’

Investigators initially ruled Wood's death an accidental drowning but reopened the case in 2011 to determine whether Wagner or anyone else played a role after the yacht's captain said he heard the couple arguing the night of her disappearance, The Associated Press reported. The Los Angeles County coroner's office amended Wood's death certificate in 2012, changing the cause of death to "drowning and other undetermined factors."

In 2018, Los Angeles County sheriff's investigators described Wagner as "a person of interest" in Wood's death. In 2022, the department said it had exhausted all leads in the case, and Wagner was no longer considered a person of interest. Wagner has long denied having any involvement in his wife's death.

Gregson Wagner said that while she was growing up, her two fathers were determined to give her a normal upbringing away from the glaring media spotlight.

"I had to do my laundry," she told the outlet. "We had dinner on the table at six o'clock. I learned how to cook in their kitchen. I learned how to do laundry. I learned how to take a bath with a hot tap and a cold tap, putting it in a pot and pouring it on my head and all these things."

Gregson Wagner also told the outlet she avoided the drugs and alcohol that have troubled some children of famous parents.

"I've definitely felt pressure in my life," Gregson Wagner said. "I know what's right, I know what's wrong. I'm not saying I haven't had very, very painful things in my life. ... But in the home, it was all very safe and secure and warm. So, I got lucky in that way."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Still, Gregson Wagner said she continues to feel the impact of losing her mother.

"When I was younger, I would get stopped on the street by people who would say things like: 'You look so much like this actress, you've probably never heard of her, but her name was Natalie Wood,'" Gregson Wagner recalled. "Most of the time I wouldn't admit I was her daughter, and just say: 'Oh, I hear that a lot!'"

"We looked so much alike and had so much in common. Where did the mother end and the child begin? We were so completely connected — and she was so sharp and perceptive — that I sometimes believed she could see right into my mind."

Gregson Wagner has been married to "7th Heaven" alum Barry Watson, 52, since 2014. They share a daughter, Clover. Gregson Wagner also launched the fragrance brand L'Amour Mere, which she says was inspired by her mother and their connection through scent.

Gregson Wagner has previously spoken about her mother's legacy.

In 2020, Gregson Wagner appeared in the HBO documentary "Natalie Wood: What Remains Behind," which featured interviews with Wood's family, close friends and confidants.

Wagner, now 96, also appeared in the documentary and discussed his relationship with Wood and her death.

The couple married in 1957 but divorced in 1962. They remarried in 1972 and were together until Wood's passing. Wagner helped raise Gregson Wagner, and he and Wood had a daughter, Courtney Wagner, who also appeared in the documentary.

"I am always blown away by his courage," Gregson Wagner told Fox News Digital at the time.

"As my dad and knowing him for basically my whole life, I know him to be such a courageous person. I was just so proud of him. I felt like he was so transparent, elegant, gracious, emotional, connected and present. He was everything that I know him to be, so it felt like an incredible experience to bear witness as his daughter. He's one of the great loves of my life. He moves me every day, and he deeply moved me on those days [of filming] for sure."

Gregson Wagner said she still has vivid, joyful memories of Wood.

"My mom made being a mom feel really effortless," Gregson Wagner said. "She loved it so much. She was always singing songs with us. We were always painting and reading. She was always there to talk to. I hear her voice a lot when I talk to [my daughter] Clover. Like, 'What are we going to do today? Are we going to take a walk?' Just the little mundane things. I can hear her voice in my ear when I talk to my own daughter."

"My parents wanted their children to have that constant feeling of being loved and nurtured — the joy of childhood," she continued. "And that's what they did. Friends came over all the time and sometimes they went out. But the focus was really on us. I think we felt really safe in their world and around them. They were able to create just a bustling, joyful, jubilant kind of atmosphere for us to grow up."

At the time, Gregson Wagner said she hoped the documentary would give viewers a fuller picture of her mother. She said the special was ultimately a celebration of Wood's life and what she accomplished both in Hollywood and as a parent.

"I hope that audiences will get a very clear picture of this woman who was so strong, funny, joyful, empowered and courageous," she said. "She had a great life. It wasn't a long one, but it was the one she wanted to have. She was the architect of her own life."

item.title: GOP accuses Walz allies of burying $52M Medicaid fraud report before election
item.description: Minnesota Republicans accuse Democrats of blocking the full Optum Medicaid fraud report, but DFL lawmakers say DHS has failed to provide it.
item.content:encoded:
Minnesota Republicans are accusing Democrats of keeping lawmakers in the dark for months about a state-commissioned Medicaid assessment that flagged more than $52 million in improper payments, arguing the delay denied them a chance to act on the report’s specific findings during the legislative session before the election.

"Fraud here has exploded under the Walz administration," Minnesota Republican Speaker of the House Lisa Demuth told Fox News Digital. "Governor Walz has held no one in his entire administration accountable for the level of fraud. It definitely brings into question what is in that report and why are they hiding it?"

The Walz administration hired Optum to conduct a third-party review of Minnesota’s Medicaid program, scrutinizing 14 high-risk services. The report identified more than $52 million in improper payments but cautioned that improper payments do not necessarily constitute "fraud, waste or abuse." The Department of Human Services released a heavily redacted version to the public in February, prompting calls from Republican lawmakers to make the full version available so they could address the risks raised during the legislative session.

"Our election here in Minnesota is 29 days away. We’re just four weeks out, and you really have to wonder why they are refusing to do this," Demuth, who is the GOP gubernatorial candidate, told Fox News Digital.

WALZ ADMINISTRATION IGNORED FRAUD WARNINGS AS BILLIONS VANISHED, HOUSE OVERSIGHT REPORT ALLEGES

Minnesota currently has a divided state legislature, with the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party (DFL) holding a slim 34-33 majority in the Senate and a rare 67-67 partisan tie in the House.

Democratic Gov. Tim Walz announced the audit in October 2025, months before allegations of widespread fraud involving members of Minnesota’s Somali diaspora drew national attention. Mounting scrutiny of the Walz administration’s handling of alleged fraud in Minnesota’s social services programs contributed to growing political pressure before Walz ended his re-election campaign in January.

WALZ'S 'EXIT INTERVIEW' REFLECTING ON HIS TENURE SPARKS LAWMAKER DEBATE ABOUT HIS LEGACY: 'NEVER SERIOUS'

Republican state Sen. Jordan Rasmusson is also accusing the Walz administration and his Democratic counterparts of seeking to "minimize" the fraud issue in the state.

"I think it’s really hard for Democrats, elected Democrats in Minnesota, to admit that we have a fraud problem of this scale, and to take accountability for those failings," Rasmusson told Fox News Digital.

The Department of Human Services said the report was heavily redacted to protect Optum’s trade secrets and prevent the release of sensitive security information that could provide criminals a "roadmap" for committing fraud.

Rasmusson introduced an amendment in April to make the full Optum report public, but it failed along party lines. A version of Rasmusson's provision was later passed in May as part of a broader budget package.

MINNESOTA'S ANTI-ICE AID FUND BECOMES LATEST CASUALTY OF STATE'S EMBARRASSING FRAUD PROBLEM

Under the law, DHS must provide the initial Optum reports to members of a legislative committee with "jurisdiction over human services policy and finance" following a joint request from the committee’s chair and ranking minority member. Lawmakers may review the report but cannot publicly release protected nonpublic information it contains.

Rasmusson said he issued a request for the full report in June. State Rep. Mohamud Noor, DFL co-chair of the Human Services Finance and Policy Committee, and former GOP House co-Chair Joe Schomacker requested the report in May. The report did not become available to a select group of lawmakers until last week.

"I'm grateful that it's out, but it's very disappointing we couldn’t have returned to St. Paul to address it," Republican state Rep. Dawn Gillman told Fox News Digital, noting that lawmakers will have to wait until January to address the report.

"The broader takeaway is that the Walz administration could have given us more access to those months ago," Rasmusson told Fox News Digital. "Legislative Democrats could have joined Republicans and got access to this information months ago during session."

However, state Sen. John Hoffman, who now has access to the report, pushed back on the notion that lawmakers needed full access to enact meaningful changes.

"This is a report about vulnerabilities in public programs," Hoffman said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Why would we release that to the public before we fixed them? We wouldn’t publish a report about which banks don’t lock their doors, either."

EXPLOSIVE SLEEPER ISSUE COULD FUEL MIDTERM SHAKEUPS, TOP REPUBLICAN PREDICTS: ‘YOU’RE GONNA SEE SURPRISES’

"The rest of us got to work passing legislation to ensure high-quality services, continuity of care for people in need and safeguards to protect against fraud," Hoffman continued. "Having reviewed the report, I can tell you it is already outdated, and the gaps and weaknesses it raises have already been addressed by laws we passed this year."

But Rasmusson, who also has the report, disagreed with Hoffman.

"After reviewing the unredacted Optum report, my main takeaway is that it underscores the systemic failures of the Walz administration and Minnesota Democrats to protect Minnesota from fraud," Rasmusson told Fox News Digital.

"Whether it is issues with determining the eligibility of program recipients, determining whether providers are actually providing real services or not, or even some of the basic analytics that would catch fraud, Minnesota is very far behind where it should be in program integrity initiatives," Rasmusson continued.

Fox News Digital reached out to DHS, which confirmed that select lawmakers now had the report.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"We appreciate legislators' interest in receiving a copy of the unredacted initial Optum report from February 2026," Minnesota Department of Human Services Temporary Commissioner John Connolly said in a statement. "In alignment with the law passed by the Legislature last session, the Minnesota Department of Human Services released the Optum reports last week."

Fox News Digital reached out to Walz's office for comment.

item.title: Ithaca council halts Cornell event permits amid scrutiny over handling of rape allegations
item.description: Ithaca Common Council voted 9-1 to block Cornell University permits over the school's handling of Jane Doe's rape allegations against fraternity members.
item.content:encoded:
The Ithaca Common Council voted late Wednesday night to stop issuing city permits to Cornell University and affiliated student groups, including fraternities, following widespread criticism of the Ivy League school's handling of rape allegations made by a former student.

After hours of debate, the council voted 9-1 in favor of a moratorium, which temporarily bars Cornell from obtaining new permits for assemblies, parades and special events at the Ithaca Commons and activities requiring noise permits, citing public safety concerns.

The measure drew support from numerous Cornell students and Ithaca residents, although some graduate students raised concerns that the restrictions were overly broad and could disrupt activities unrelated to Greek life.

CORNELL PROTESTERS SWARM CAMPUS TO SUPPORT JANE DOE, CALL FOR UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT'S RESIGNATION

One graduate student warned that the moratorium could result in canceled or delayed events, lost deposits, reduced access to venues and disruptions to conferences.

The moratorium will stay in place until Nov. 5, unless the council extends it at a later date. The measure also includes an amendment that requires Cornell to refer investigations involving sexual and violent crimes to the Ithaca Police Department, though its unclear how that will be enforced.

The moratorium comes after the student, identified as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit in September accusing seven former Chi Phi fraternity members of drugging and raping her on the night of Oct. 19, 2024, and into the following morning.

In the lawsuit, she alleges she arrived at the frat house already intoxicated, after which the men pressured her into taking ketamine and other substances. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated.

CORNELL PICKS FORMER DEPUTY US ATTORNEY GENERAL TO REVIEW SEX ASSAULT RESPONSE

The fraternity was suspended on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day Doe reported sexual assault allegations to campus police, according to Doe's civil complaint.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who initially declined to pursue charges, has said Doe's Nov. 2024 sworn statement did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang-raped and, instead, described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as "voluntary, conscious, and consensual."

However, CBS New York obtained the transcript of the Cornell police interviews with Jane Doe on Nov. 14 and 15, 2024, during which she told investigators: "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."

Van Houten said he was never provided the full transcript. Late last month, he announced his office was reopening the case because the allegations contained in Jane Doe's lawsuit differed from her sworn statement nearly two years earlier.

BAR NAMED IN CORNELL RAPE LAWSUIT DISPUTES ACCUSER'S ACCOUNT, SAYS SHE WAS NEVER SERVED ALCOHOL WHILE UNDERAGE

In an interview with The Associated Press on Wednesday, Jane Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said Cornell police led her to believe the criminal investigation remained active even though Van Houten had decided against filing charges just days after she first spoke with investigators.

Van Houten has said he instructed Cornell police to inform Jane Doe that charges would not be pursued, but acknowledged he never spoke directly with her or her attorney.

Gov. Kathy Hochul effectively took the investigation out of Van Houten's hands on Oct. 1, by appointing Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor on the case.

"Newly released information continues to raise serious questions about the investigation conducted by the Cornell Police Department and the decision by the Tompkins County District Attorney not to prosecute an alleged sexual assault on Cornell University's campus in October 2024," Hochul said in a statement.

She added: "This has, in turn, undercut my faith, and the public's faith, in the District Attorney's ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time."

On Wednesday, one of the men named in Jane Doe's lawsuit petitioned a court to remove James from the case, accusing her of bias over a social media post she made days before her appointment in which she called what Doe allegedly endured "horrific and unacceptable," The Associated Press reported.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Luke Grimes says he hasn't spoken to Kevin Costner since 'Yellowstone'
item.description: Luke Grimes revealed he hasn't spoken to Kevin Costner since their "Yellowstone" days ended and seriously doubts the actor would ever appear on "Marshals."
item.content:encoded:
Luke Grimes and Kevin Costner haven't spoken since their time on "Yellowstone."

During an interview with USA Today, Grimes explained that their relationship did not continue once Costner left the Taylor Sheridan series in 2024.

The outlet asked Grimes if Costner would ever make an appearance on his show, "Marshals," which Grimes shot down. "I haven't talked to Kevin since we stopped working together. Not for any reason other than we're busy guys and life moves on," he said.

TAYLOR SHERIDAN SAYS HOLLYWOOD DIDN’T BELIEVE IN YELLOWSTONE, NOW IT’S A TV EMPIRE

Grimes admitted it would be "cool" if Costner joined "Marshals," but he "doubts" that would ever happen.

"If there was a flashback, I would probably rather it be with Monica [Kelsey Asbille] than John. I think that would be more poignant to the character, but we'll see," Grimes said.

Grimes and Costner starred in "Yellowstone" for four seasons together. Costner played John Dutton, the powerful patriarch of the Dutton family and owner of the Yellowstone Ranch, one of the largest cattle ranches in the United States.

Grimes played Kayce Dutton, John’s youngest son and a former Navy SEAL. In their series, Kayce was caught between his family’s ranching legacy and the life he wants with his wife, Monica, and their son, Tate.

Grimes took his "Yellowstone" character to Sheridan's spinoff series, "Marshals." The series shows Kayce after he leaves the ranch and joins an elite unit of U.S. Marshals in Montana.

Costner’s exit from "Yellowstone" followed a long-running scheduling dispute as production delays collided with his work on "Horizon: An American Saga." item.title: California woman accused of spying for China fights detention with $820K in proposed security
item.description: Wanying Zhang offered over $800,000 in property equity for bail after her arrest while boarding a flight to China on unregistered agent charges.
item.content:encoded:
A California real estate agent accused of gathering intelligence on a relative of Taiwan's president for the Chinese government sought release from federal custody Wednesday, offering more than $800,000 in property equity and financial guarantees while disputing prosecutors' claims that she posed a flight risk.

Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine, argued through her attorney that her American citizenship, family ties and history of returning from overseas trips demonstrated she would appear for future court proceedings, according to a nine-page defense filing obtained by Fox News Digital.

Zhang was arrested Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport while preparing to board a flight to China. She faces a federal charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.

FEDS SAY US CITIZEN GATHERED INFORMATION ON AMERICAN TARGETS FOR CHINESE COMMUNIST PARTY

Her attorney, Craig Harbaugh, told the court that Zhang came to the United States in 2014, became a naturalized citizen in 2020 and has worked in Orange County real estate for approximately a decade.

She lives with her husband and their two daughters, ages 8 and 5, according to the filing.

The defense proposed using an Irvine residence with at least $700,000 in equity to secure her release, along with $120,000 in financial guarantees from her husband, his sister, his father and a family friend.

Harbaugh also proposed GPS-monitored home detention, surrendering travel documents, electronic-device monitoring and restrictions on entering airports or contacting individuals connected to the case.

The defense acknowledged that Pretrial Services recommended detention over concerns about Zhang's potential failure to appear in court, but argued that strict release conditions would adequately address those concerns.

Zhang's lawyers also disputed the significance of her one-way ticket to China, arguing that she frequently booked international trips using separately purchased outbound and return flights.

According to the filing, Zhang had traveled to China, France and Japan during the past year and returned to the United States after each trip.

The defense said her planned October trip was intended to visit her mother and had been postponed until after her daughters' birthdays.

TAIWAN ANALYSTS SAY TRUMP-XI SUMMIT PRODUCED NO POLICY SHIFT BUT REAL TEST LIES AHEAD

The underlying criminal complaint alleges Zhang participated in a September 2025 surveillance operation outside the Seattle-area residence of a close relative of a Taiwanese government official.

According to an FBI affidavit, investigators reviewed security-camera footage allegedly showing Zhang and another individual photographing the person and family members near their home.

Federal authorities also alleged that Zhang transmitted photographs, video and vehicle information to a suspected Chinese government official through electronic communications.

Investigators said Zhang attended China's University of International Relations in Beijing, which the FBI described as closely associated with China's intelligence apparatus.

Zhang's attorneys contest the charge and maintain that she intends to establish her innocence.

She faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in federal prison if convicted.

item.title: Weaponizing the charge of genocide fuels an increasingly dangerous antisemitism
item.description: Genocide accusations against Israel are dangerously misused, U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum leaders say, as violent antisemitism surges globally.
item.content:encoded:
Genocide, the intentional annihilation of a group of people, is the gravest of crimes. As malicious actors weaponize the term and endanger Jews everywhere, meticulous use of the charge is more essential than ever.

We are honored to serve as the current and former chairs of the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, an institution memorializing history’s most well-documented genocide: Nazi Germany and its collaborators’ attempt to systematically murder every Jewish man, woman and child in Europe. They almost succeeded. Two-thirds of European Jews – 6 million – were killed. The global Jewish population has yet to recover, with fewer Jews alive today than in 1939, when World War II began.

Holocaust survivors fervently hoped antisemitism would wither when Germany was defeated and its crimes exposed. Yet, they knew from centuries of persecutions long before the Nazis, this ancient hatred is impossible to eradicate. Even so, after World War II, antisemitism became socially unacceptable. The shocking reactions from many quarters to Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack on Israel, three years ago, show this is no longer the case.

DANNY DANON: FROM OCT 7 TO FLIGHT 1073: THE RESILIENCE THAT KEEPS ISRAEL STANDING

On that day, Hamas terrorists invaded Israel intending to murder as many Jewish people as possible, bringing about the deadliest day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust. As Israel defends itself, we reiterate our wholehearted conviction that Israel has not committed genocide, reflecting the United States government’s consistent and prevailing view.

At the same time, we cannot forget the terrible tragedy many innocent Gazans have experienced as a result of the war. The loss of tens of thousands, including many children, is horrific.

'NOBODY WANTS THIS': CONSULTING RABBI CALLS OUT STAR'S 'IGNORANT' TAKE ON 'GENOCIDE' IN GAZA

As we mourn so many innocent lives lost, we cannot ignore that Hamas puts civilians in harm’s way as a central part of its strategy to demonize Israel. Despite this deadly strategy, Israel has made efforts to warn civilians when to evacuate, provide food and relief, and facilitate vaccine distribution.

Israel, like any country, is not exempt from criticism. And yet, whether out of ignorance or malice, people from all walks of life, often with little knowledge or legal expertise, including in the specific definition of genocide, continually wield the term. Others weaponize it to delegitimize the world’s only Jewish state. Regardless of their intention, the impact is a terrifying eruption of antisemitism and a more dangerous world for Jewish people everywhere.

ISRAELI PRESIDENT HERZOG CALLS ANTISEMITISM A 'CONTAMINATION OF SOCIETIES' AS HATE CRIMES SURGE

Furthermore, state actors like Iran, Qatar, China and Russia spread antisemitic and anti-Israel conspiracy theories and Holocaust denial to stir hatred of Jews and sow chaos in democracies. They are succeeding. Antisemitism is no longer lurking at society’s fringes. It is marching openly through its institutions. Violent antisemitism is at levels not seen since the Holocaust. From Pittsburgh’s Tree of Life synagogue to Bondi Beach in Australia, to Manchester, England, and far too many other places, Jews are under deadly attack. And every day, Jews face relentless harassment and threats on streets, campuses and online.

The Holocaust teaches the dangers of unchecked antisemitism and how hatred began with the Jews but did not end with the Jews – it infected all of society. It is a sad truth that as Jews desperately tried to flee Nazi Europe, the rest of the world did not want them, including our own nation.

History shows some Jews who survived returned to their homes only to face further deadly violence from their former neighbors. Knowing Europe was a Jewish graveyard, survivors desperately wanted to build new lives where they could feel secure – primarily the United States and their ancestral homeland, what is now Israel, which was then under British colonial rule.

The Holocaust also teaches other lessons about humanity. As the Nazis and their collaborators hunted Jews, in every country some remarkable individuals chose to help, rising above the propaganda, hatred and threats to their own safety. And the survivors showed remarkable resilience as they rebuilt their lives, perhaps wondering if there had been a Jewish state, how many of their lost family members might have been saved.

Even today, principled individuals are risking all to stand against this age-old hatred. Holocaust survivors, people who have seen the worst humanity has to offer, continue to demonstrate a strength and courage we can only marvel at as they share their testimony. We need this courage from all of society.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

History has taught us what happens when antisemitism is excused, normalized or allowed to masquerade as something more respectable. We cannot make that mistake again. "Never Again" cannot be something we say about the past. It must be a promise of what all of us are willing to do in the present.

We owe that to the 6 million. We owe it to the Holocaust survivors still among us. And we owe it to the generations of Jews who must never again be taught that hatred is simply something they are expected to endure.

Ambassador Stuart Eizenstat served as chair of the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum under President Joe Biden.

item.title: What strangers can learn from your political donation
item.description: Federal Election Commission records can expose your name, address, employer and donation history once contributions exceed the $200 threshold.
item.content:encoded:
Search your name in the Federal Election Commission's contribution database or on a campaign finance site such as OpenSecrets.org. If you have given enough to trigger federal disclosure requirements, you may be surprised by how much information can be connected to your donation. Depending on the record, that can include your name, mailing address, employer, occupation, donation amount and the political committee that received your money.

This is not a data breach. It is part of federal campaign finance disclosure law. And once information about you is public, it can potentially be combined with personal details found elsewhere online. Here's what your political donation can reveal, how that information can be used and what you can do to reduce the rest of your exposure.

Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.

Federal campaigns generally must itemize an individual's contributions once that person's contributions exceed $200 in the aggregate during the applicable election cycle. For PACs and party committees, the reporting period can be based on the calendar year.

An itemized federal contribution can include:

One contribution may not seem revealing on its own. The privacy concern grows when those details can be connected with information already available through people-search sites, public records and data brokers.

Pay particular attention to your employer and occupation. A people-search profile may already include addresses and relatives, while a campaign finance record can add another verified detail about where you work or what you do. Want to see how much of your personal information is already exposed online? Use the free data exposure scanner at CyberGuy.com to check.

A campaign finance record alone provides only part of the picture. Other public sources and people-search sites may reveal much more. Sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified can contain address histories, possible relatives, phone numbers, email addresses and property information. When information from several sources lines up, someone researching you may be able to build a much more detailed profile. Here is how those pieces can connect.

Names are rarely unique. An address, employer or occupation can help distinguish you from another person with the same name. That makes publicly available information useful for confirming that someone has found the right person.

Once someone has your name and location, people-search services may make it easier to identify possible relatives. Your political donation record does not normally list your family members. However, information found elsewhere can connect your identity with a spouse, adult child, parent or other relative. That can create opportunities for impersonation scams and highly personalized phishing attempts.

HOW HURRICANE CHARITY SCAMS TARGET YOU BEFORE STORMS HIT

Knowing where you work gives a scammer another detail that can make an email, text or phone call feel legitimate. A phishing message that mentions your actual employer or professional role can be more convincing than a generic message because it contains information you recognize. That is why limiting the amount of personal information available across the web can reduce what criminals have to work with.

Scammers frequently imitate legitimate organizations, charities and fundraising groups. The FTC warns that fraudulent fundraisers may use familiar-sounding names, pressure people to act quickly or falsely claim someone donated before. There is also an important legal protection around federal campaign finance data. Information copied or obtained from FEC reports about individual contributors cannot legally be sold or used to solicit political or charitable contributions or for commercial purposes. Criminals do not always follow the law, of course. Still, you should be suspicious of any unexpected fundraising request that seems unusually familiar with your personal history.

Using an online fundraising platform does not automatically make a federal contribution private. For earmarked federal contributions exceeding $200, reporting requirements can include the contributor's name, mailing address, employer, occupation, date and amount.

State campaign finance rules are different. Disclosure thresholds and the information made public vary by state, so a contribution that is not itemized under federal rules could still be subject to separate state reporting requirements.

This is an important limitation to understand. A data removal service generally cannot erase legally required government records such as federal campaign finance filings. That means an FEC filing is not something a removal service can simply delete. What these services can address is the personal information surrounding that public record.

Your campaign finance record might identify your name, mailing address, employer and occupation. Meanwhile, data brokers may have phone numbers, email addresses, relatives, previous addresses and other personal information. Removing those additional profiles can make it harder for someone to connect separate pieces of information about you into one detailed profile.

Some data removal services automatically send opt-out requests to data brokers and continue checking for information that may reappear. Others also offer custom removal requests for websites where your personal information is exposed. However, legal and technical restrictions still apply, especially when the information comes from government records or other sources that are required to remain public.

You can also submit removal requests yourself. The process takes more time, but reducing the amount of personal information spread across people-search sites and data brokers can make it harder for strangers or scammers to build a detailed profile about you. Here are several steps I would take to see what information about you is already exposed.

Start by searching your name through the FEC's campaign finance records and OpenSecrets.org. Look closely at what information is associated with your contributions. Do not assume every result belongs to you, especially if you have a common name.

THE SECRET LIST THAT TELLS SCAMMERS YOU'RE AN EASY TARGET

For federal candidate committees, individual contributions generally become itemized once your aggregate contributions exceed $200 during an election cycle. PAC and party committee reporting rules can use a calendar-year threshold instead. Also remember that some committees voluntarily disclose contributions below the amount they are required to itemize.

State disclosure laws vary significantly. Your state may use a different reporting threshold or disclose different information than the federal system, so check the campaign finance database maintained by your state election authority.

Do not assume a message is legitimate because it mentions a candidate, organization or contribution you recognize. Instead of clicking a link in an unexpected email or text, visit the organization's official website independently. Also be wary of anyone pressuring you to donate immediately or asking you to pay through gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency.

You may not be able to remove a legally required campaign finance filing, but you can reduce the additional information available about you through data brokers and people-search sites. You can submit opt-out requests yourself or use a data removal service to handle many of those requests for you. I think the surprising part here is how much information can become connected to something as simple as making a political contribution. Federal disclosure rules can make your name, mailing address, employer, occupation and contribution history publicly available once you cross the reporting threshold. You cannot erase a legally required FEC filing with a data removal service, but you can reduce the other information surrounding it. I would search my own name, see what is visible and then work on removing the people-search and data broker profiles that make it easier for strangers or scammers to fill in the rest of the picture.

item.title: Olivia Rodrigo calls women-focused festival ‘one hundred percent’ political, tells critics to not buy a ticket
item.description: Olivia Rodrigo confirmed Daisy Chain Fields was "one hundred percent" political, raising $20 million for Planned Parenthood and other charities.
item.content:encoded:
Grammy-winning singer Olivia Rodrigo said her women-focused music festival Daisy Chain Fields was "one hundred percent" political, saying critics who disagree with her message "don’t have to buy a ticket."

Headlined by Rodrigo, the one-day music festival in Irvine, Calif., featured an all-female lineup, including performances by Chappell Roan, Sarah McLachlan and Stevie Nicks.

Net proceeds from Daisy Chain Fields were directed toward nonprofit organizations "dedicated to advancing and advocating for women and girls," including Planned Parenthood, the Center for Reproductive Rights, Baby2Baby and the Black Mamas Matter Alliance.

The festival raised $20 million for the women-focused charities and Rodrigo made it clear that she planned the festival with politics in mind.

PLANNED PARENTHOOD ACROSS MIDWEST AT RISK DUE TO LACK OF FEDERAL FUNDS AFTER 3 FACILITIES CLOSE IN MICHIGAN

"One hundred percent, yes," she told The Hollywood Reporter when asked whether Daisy Chain Fields was political.

"But I think it’s also about joy," she added. "I think the two things can exist at the same time, they kind of have to… I think young people have lost hope in our leaders and lost hope in each other. I really wanted to galvanize people and be evidence of what can happen when you come together and are part of something and contribute."

The "Drivers License" singer also stated that those who don't agree with the festival's political message don't have to buy a ticket.

"Everyone is welcome to come to Daisy Chain. But if you don’t agree with the message that we’re sending, then you don’t have to buy a ticket," she said.

ED SHEERAN CONCERTGOERS WARN ARTISTS ABOUT SHARING POLITICAL VIEWS: 'YOU'RE GOING TO ALIENATE' FANS

Daisy Chain Fields was inspired by Lilith Fair, an all-female traveling music festival launched in the late 1990s by McLachlan, who was frustrated over the lack of female representation in the music industry.

Rodrigo, 23, argued that women had more rights in the 1990s than they do in 2026.

"When Lilith Fair was happening 30 years ago, women in America had more rights, had more autonomy over their bodies," the singer said.

"I’ve always felt really protective of my young fans, and when I play a show and I look out into the audience and see young girls with their friends or their moms or their families, I feel such a kinship with them," she continued. "And if I could be a small part in making the world a safer and better place for them to grow up and live, that’s what I want."

SUPREME COURT TEMPORARILY BLOCKS APPEALS COURT RULING ON ABORTION PILL, RESTORES WIDER ACCESS TO DRUG

Rodrigo released her song "Serena Joy" just before the festival. The single is named after a character from "Handmaid’s Tale" who promoted an oppressive regime that eventually deprived her of her own power.

The lyrics, including "a tower we built, painted gold on the walls" and "now go bother your neighbors while we do what we wish," have prompted speculation that the song takes aim at President Donald Trump, though Rodrigo declined to confirm that interpretation.

"It’s basically a song about complacency," the singer said. "It’s about how an attack on one person’s human rights is an attack on all of our human rights. It’s something I’ve been thinking about a lot."

Rodrigo's decision to incorporate politics into her performances drew praise and criticism from political commentators, some of whom argued that her approach alienates fans who do not share her views.

Podcast host Ben Ferguson told Fox News Digital that the festival represented the "breathtaking hypocrisy of Hollywood," arguing that Rodrigo was treating her audience like "political minions."

SPRINGSTEEN, OTHER STARS SHARE STAGE WITH HARDCORE LEFTIST GROUPS AT MUSIC FEST

"These celebrities love preaching tolerance, diversity and inclusion right up until someone dares to disagree with their politics. Then suddenly it’s, ‘Don’t buy a ticket.’ Apparently, everyone is welcome as long as they think exactly like Olivia Rodrigo," Ferguson said. "That’s not inclusion. That’s political arrogance wrapped in a concert tour."

But Rodrigo’s willingness to openly embrace politics has also won praise from Democrats, including strategist Kaivan Shroff, who said celebrities who don’t speak out on current events can be viewed as "inauthentic."

"This is not some niche artist trying to cultivate a fanbase by leaning into cheap politics. She is making politics part of the art, part of the live show and part of the brand, and at least she is being honest about that and owning it," Shroff told Fox News Digital.

"I actually think ‘if you don’t agree, don’t buy a ticket’ is cleaner than pretending the politics are incidental. But there is a tradeoff," he continued. "The minute you tell people the show itself carries a political message, disagreement with that message becomes part of the consumer experience too. You cannot make politics central to the product and then act surprised when the product gets judged politically."

Rodrigo has previously sparred with the Trump administration, condemning the Department of Homeland Security in 2025 after it used her song "All-American B----" in a social media post encouraging illegal immigrants to self-deport from the country. She has also criticized Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for being "barbaric and cruel."

Film critic and Hollywood in Toto founder Christian Toto echoed Ferguson’s concerns, telling Fox News Digital: "In these contentious times, getting hyper political and alienating large swathes of your audience is less than ideal."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Hecklers interrupt Trump Texas rally multiple times
item.description: President Donald Trump claimed protesters at his San Antonio rally were paid by enemies of the nation as he urged supporters to back Ken Paxton.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump did not let multiple protesters step on his messaging in Texas on Wednesday night; in fact, he used the moments to claim that a Democrat-run city is using America's own freedom of speech to spread a left-wing agenda against his administration in the midterm elections.

"You know, many of these protesters are paid — you know that, right?" Trump told the packed Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio. "Because you come in and, you know, they'll have like this perfect shirt on, made by the best printer money can buy."

"I love where they all have the same exact size, beautiful pink and purple and blue and all different colors. And they're perfect, made by the same printer, very expensive signs," he added.

TRUMP TOUTS ‘GOLDEN AGE’ AT OHIO RALLY, URGES VOTERS TO DELIVER GOP MIDTERM WINS

"They don't make these signs. These are paid protesters," Trump claimed. "They're paid by enemies of our nation. No, I'm telling you, they pay them for this."

Trump pivoted to his supporters who came out to rally with him for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, some waving cowboy hats.

GOP FACES BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS REPUBLICANS PAINT ELECTION AS ‘COMPETITION WITH COMMUNISM’

As the crowd chanted "USA," drowning out several protesters who interrupted the event multiple times in a Texas city led by a Democrat, Trump added, "If there are any more paid protesters, please raise your hand and get the hell out of here."

Trump is urging his base to turn out as if he is on the ballot in the midterms — because, as he says, the ability to pass his agenda in Congress is and his backers must help keep Congress in Republican hands.

"We will not allow our country, our culture, our history and our heritage to be looted and plundered anymore," Trump said.

"What they did to this country," Trump continued, pointing back to former President Joe Biden and his 2024 opponent Kamala Harris, "I said the other day, if Kamala won — or if that ideology won, forget about Kamala — if that ideology won, I don't believe we'd have a country anymore. I don't believe it. And now we have the hottest country anywhere in the world."

REPUBLICAN CAVALRY ARRIVES FOR KEN PAXTON AS BIG-BUCKS TEXAS OFFENSIVE OPENS CASH FLOODGATES

The battle for the Texas Senate seat between Paxton and Democrat James Talarico is one of the midterm battlegrounds that could determine Trump's fate in his final two years in office.

"I will not let my legacy of having the highest vote in the history of Texas be tarnished or destroyed by allowing that travesty to happen again," he continued. "If they get in and do that and remember, like a guy like Talarico, it's basically one vote. It's so important — forget about for Texas, it's still just one vote — it's a killer in Congress because we have a very close majority. We can't let that happen.

"If they get in, they will open your borders and let the entire world pour into our country like they did before. And we can't let that happen. We're not going to let it happen again."

At least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president, including one who appeared to be close to the stage. Some were led away by police. Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption.

TRUMP FIRES BACK AFTER PROTESTER INTERRUPTS MYRTLE BEACH RALLY FOR GRAHAM: 'MOM IS VOTING FOR US'

"You know, I never talk about looks of a person, but those are really bad-looking people," Trump said about one protester. "You have to say they are bad-looking people. Come on."

"No, he's going back to home to mom right now," Trump quipped. "What he doesn't know is that his mom voted for Trump."

TRUMP-LINKED MAGA INC POURS $10M INTO KEN PAXTON'S TEXAS SENATE RACE AGAINST JAMES TALARICO

Trump was in San Antonio for his third trip to Texas in less than a month as Republicans try to stave off Democratic gains in the nation’s most populous red state.

item.title: Caitlin Clark joins Pat McAfee on ESPN's 'College GameDay,' and left-wing podcasters have a problem with it
item.description: Caitlin Clark's return to Iowa for "College GameDay" drew record October ratings, but two podcast hosts questioned her appearance with Pat McAfee.
item.content:encoded:
Caitlin Clark went back to Iowa on Saturday to promote her new Nike shoe and make picks on ESPN’s "College GameDay." The show drew its biggest audience of the season and the biggest October audience in its 40-season history.

Over at "The Sports Gossip Show," a podcast hosted by two women named Charlotte Wilder and Madeline Hill, the hosts found reasons to question the appearance, including Clark sitting alongside Pat McAfee.

I wrote about their show in August after they mocked Riley Gaines and called Sophie Cunningham’s defense of women’s sports a "right-wing grift." So, you have a good idea of where they stand politically.

Their podcast was distributed by the New York Times-owned Athletic for about a year before they announced their departure in August. Left-wing outlet Awful Announcing described their departure as part of a "broader exodus of podcast stars" from the New York Times. I must have missed the part where these two became stars.

CAITLIN CLARK IS MISSING FROM ESPN' S NEW WNBA DOCUMENTARY AND THE FILMMAKERS WON' T SAY WHY

On the episode, Wilder suggested Caitlin Clark needed to do something "for her own PR." So, Clark got a national platform to promote her shoe, helped drive millions of viewers to the show, and she should be concerned about her PR?

I think she’ll be OK.

"Pat McAfee, in 2024, called Caitlin a ‘white b---.’ Which I could give you the context for, but it doesn’t really matter," Wilder said during the episode.

Members of the media often leave out context that hurts their narrative, but they’re not usually so upfront about it. I guess it's refreshing that Wilder admits she's willing to eschew basic journalistic ethics for the sake of the story she prefers to tell.

I happen to think the context does matter, so here it is. McAfee did call Clark a "white b—-" during his show in 2024 but he was defending Clark.

His argument was that people needed to stop crediting the entire rookie class for attention that she was bringing to the WNBA. He was also pushing back on the suggestion that fans liked her simply because she was white. He wanted people to acknowledge how good she was and what she was doing for the league.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

McAfee apologized for his wording, explained that he meant it as a compliment and said Clark accepted his apology. Wilder acknowledged that McAfee had apologized.

The podcast host stopped short of saying Clark shouldn’t have done "GameDay," but still questioned her decision to share a stage with McAfee. Clark is allowed to decide she’s comfortable with him. Why does she need to answer to two podcast hosts about an apology she reportedly accepted over two years ago?

Wilder not only wants Clark to answer for appearances on GameDay, but also wants her to keep addressing something she's addressed multiple times.

"We’ve just said before, if you and I were in a situation where a bunch of Black women were getting death threats and having a really hard time because of people who said they were fans of ours, I think we would say, ‘You are not a fan of mine if you are perpetuating this behavior and these actions.’ It’s not the hardest thing in the world to say," Wilder said, arguing that Clark should say "something a little more forceful."

Here’s Clark in September 2024:

"Nobody in our league should be facing any sort of racism, hurtful, disrespectful, hateful comments and threats," she said. "Those aren’t fans, those are trolls."

And in May 2025, here's Clark responding to a question about an alleged racist incident at a Fever game (the claim was never substantiated):

"There’s no place for that in our game, there’s no place for that in society."

And then again in July 2026:

"Harassment, hate, none of that is OK."

Does she need to open every news conference with it, or would once a week satisfy these two?

Wilder even acknowledged Clark had spoken out before, but reduced her comments to a general call for everyone to be treated the same. Clark explicitly condemned racism and threats and said, "Those aren’t fans, those are trolls." Wilder sure does love leaving out important context, huh?

And why does Clark have to keep answering for online trolls in the first place? Random people on the internet don't get to make Clark their spokesperson just by calling themselves fans of hers.

Their discussion also included Kelsey Mitchell’s complaints about the scrutiny surrounding the Fever. I wrote about those comments Sunday, and the benefits of all that attention belong in the conversation.

WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT

Mitchell earned $1.4 million in WNBA salary this season, according to Spotrac. That’s more than the roughly $1.12 million she earned in her first eight seasons combined. Her play earned her the contract but Clark helped grow the audience for a league that can now pay players that kind of money.

That’s a substantial contribution to her fellow players, many of whom are the Black women who Wilder and Hill think Clark needs to spend more time protecting.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"I do think she could do something at the very least for her own PR," Wilder said.

Of all the things Wilder said that were outrageous, this might have been the most outlandish. Caitlin Clark is the most popular female athlete on the planet. Fever games draw more viewers than any other team in the WNBA.

Clark is a spokesperson for major brands like State Farm and Gatorade. Her first signature Nike shoe nearly sold out on Nike’s website within two hours of its release.

So what, exactly, does Clark need to do differently? Bow down to the left-wing media mob to appease podcasters like Wilder and Hill?

Saturday’s "GameDay" averaged 2.9 million viewers, according to ESPN. It was the most-watched episode of the season and the most-watched October episode in the show’s history. The final hour, in which Clark appeared, averaged 3.7 million viewers.

For the record, "The Sports Gossip Show" averaged about 7,200 YouTube views across 39 episodes spanning roughly five months. If anyone needs some PR advice, it's these two.

Although, I’d love to hear the pitch to Clark’s PR team after that weekend.

"Sorry about all the people watching your client promote her shoe. Have you considered getting her to issue another statement about racism? There's this podcast that no one watches that would really appreciate it. Thanks."

item.title: MLW star Donovan Dijak hopes to tag with former partner who left for WWE after lengthy title reign
item.description: Donovan Dijak reveals his hope to reunite with Baron Corbin after their 317-day MLW tag team title reign spanning Mexico, Australia, and beyond.
item.content:encoded:
Donovan Dijak and Bishop Dyer had a lengthy reign as Major League Wrestling (MLW) tag team champions, sharing it with Josh Bishop as well under the Freebird Rule which allowed any members of the trio to hold and defend the belts.

The group, collectively known as The Skyscrapers, had the titles for 317 days. As Dyer left MLW for WWE, Dijak and Bishop held the titles until losing the belts on a summer episode of "Fusion" to The Good Brothers.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

With Dyer now in WWE and a former WWE United States champion almost immediately upon his return there, Dijak looked back on his reign with the competitor fondly. He told OutKick Dropkick he wants to team up with Dyer again somewhere down the line.

"I love everything that I was able to do with Bishop Dyer, now Baron Corbin, and tag teaming with him was unbelievable levels of fun," he said. "We got to do it in Mexico. We got to do it in Australia. We got to do it all over the United States, which was great for me, especially from a guy like him at his level. He didn't take like a ton of indie dates. He was doing sort of limited appearances, but I was a part of a ton of that. So, to be able to have that experience with him, and I worked with him in WWE before, I just can't wait to tag with him again.

"I don't know when and where it's going to happen. I hope that it does happen because that's like kind of how pro wrestling works. You never know when your last time tagging with someone or your last time wrestling someone is going to be. Every time you work with someone, your brain always goes, oh man, I can't wait to do that again, and where are we going to do it and stuff like that. And then sometimes it's just like, oh, they're retired, I guess it's never happening again or, in some like horrible cases, sometimes, the person you're working with unfortunately passes away or something, which, sadly, happened to me way too many times in the world of professional wrestling, and that hits on an entirely different level in terms of I'm never going to be able to see that person again. But sometimes you leave a locker room and you're like, I'll see these guys all, and then you never see them for another year or two."

Dijak and Dyer had multiple title defenses during their reign. They defeated Averno and Euforia at CMLL Viernes Espectacular and they beat The Good Brothers earlier this year after winning the belts at last year’s Summer of the Beasts against Magnus and Rugido.

Dijak suggested he wouldn’t trade any of that for the world.

"There's so many of those experiences. I just hope that he and I get to tag together again because we had an incredible run in MLW," he told OutKick Dropkick. "We were the MLW tag team champions, and he's just a good friend. We still talk all the time. I hope it happens again."

Now, Dijak and is partnered with Bishop as The Skyscrapers continue to forge their own path in MLW.
