item.title: Peyton Manning's freshman son gets rocked, but fans are more stunned at all the scholarship offers
item.description: Peyton Manning's son Marshall Manning already has four Division I offers as a freshman QB, including Miami and Ohio State, despite limited playing time.
item.content:encoded:
All aboard the Marshall Manning hype train! Sure, it won't arrive until 2030, but we're getting a head start just in case there's any traffic along the way.

While one Manning is about to leave college football for the NFL, the next in line is already waiting in the shadows.

Yep. You read that right.

Peyton Manning's son is slowly making his way onto the field for Baylor School (Chattanooga) — one of the top football programs in the country.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

I've written about Manning before this season, way back in Week 1 when he saw the field, briefly, in the season-opener. It's been pretty quiet on the Manning front since, but the freshman started bubbling back up last weekend ... for multiple different reasons.

For starters, he did see some legit playing time in Baylor's blowout win over McCallie, playing all of the fourth quarter in mop-up duty. the freshman played well, completing a couple passes, leading a scoring drive, and getting his bell rung along the way.

This is how you step into a throw, folks:

BOOM!

Good hit, better throw. I can still remember Peyton Manning getting his doors blown off and still, somehow, dropping pass after pass right in the bucket. It was amazing.

Like father, like son!

TEXAS OPENS SEASON AGAINST TEXAS STATE AS ARCH MANNING FACES A MAKE-OR-BREAK COLLEGE FOOTBALL YEAR

Although, to be fair, Peyton would've spent 40 seconds audibling to the correct protection so he avoided that sort of hit. Marshall will learn. High school football play clocks are only so long.

All in all, it was a fine night for Manning. Baylor cruised to a win, he completed some passes along the way, and finally saw some real playing time behind Ole Miss commit, Keegan Croucher.

See? Nothing special, but still, some experience. That's all you want as a freshman, right? Well, that and a few scholarship offers would be nice ...

Don't worry! Marshall has nothing to worry about on that front.

Believe it or not, the freshman QB already has four Division I offers despite barely playing a down this season. Four!

According to 247 Sports — which tracks these sort of things — Manning has already received offers from Miami, Ohio State, Purdue and Missouri State. Not bad for a 15-year-old.

Not bad for a kid who hasn't even thrown his first high school touchdown yet!

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

What a time to be alive.

Look, obviously it has a little something to do with his last name. We saw that with Arch Manning's insane recruitment as well. If your last name is Manning, teams are probably gonna be more willing to take a chance on you. Rightfully so.

But we also live in a new age of college football. The NIL era. The transfer portal era. This ain't the world I grew up in. It's certainly not the world Peyton or Eli grew up in.

Teams like Miami and Ohio State have all the money in the world to throw at these kids ... for now. We'll see how this new bill from congress shakes things up when it finally passes in 2040 (roughly).

Why not make him an offer during his freshman season just to get on the board? You know you'll have the money when the time actually comes to be serious about it, so what's the harm?

Not sure little 'ol Missouri State's gonna be able to compete with the boosters in Columbus, but I do appreciate the effort.

Regardless, none of this really matters until 2030. We've still got a lot of Marshall Manning recruiting in front of us, folks. A lot.

Frankly, we're just getting started.

item.title: Massive 2,000-year-old discovery from time of Jesus emerges remarkably intact
item.description: A 25-ton mikveh from the Second Temple period was extracted intact from Kiryat Gat, revealing a previously unknown Jewish settlement near Jerusalem. Author Dinesh D'Souza weighed in.
item.content:encoded:
A remarkably intact 2,000-year-old Jewish ritual bath dating to around the time of Jesus has been unearthed in Israel — shedding light not only on Christ's life but also "illuminating the world of the Bible," according to a bestselling author and filmmaker.

The mikveh, which dates to the Second Temple period roughly 2,000 years ago, was recently extracted from Kiryat Gat, an Israeli city roughly 35 miles southwest of Jerusalem.

The structure had been uncovered during an archaeological excavation. The operation to remove it intact was announced by the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) in September.

JESUS' CRUCIFIXION ACCOUNT GETS FRESH LOOK AFTER ANCIENT RING TIED TO PILATE IS REINTERPRETED

Pictures released by officials show a massive crane lifting the 25-ton mikveh intact from the archaeological site.

Mikvehs, or Jewish ritual baths, are traditionally used for purification.

The bath dates roughly to the time of the life and ministry of Jesus Christ, who, as a Jew living during the Second Temple period, likely used mikvehs, though Scripture does not explicitly say that he did.

The mikveh is evidence that a Second Temple-period Jewish settlement, previously unknown to scholars, once existed in the area, according to officials.

JESUS’ GALILEE MINISTRY SITE REVEALS RARE, TINY STONE AFTER STUDENT'S SURPRISING FIND

Officials also noted that the excavation uncovered stone measuring vessels, which were widely used during the Second Temple period because, under Jewish law, they were not considered susceptible to ritual impurity.

The ancient structure is eventually expected to return to the community where it was found.

"The operation was carried out with the aim of protecting the ancient structure from damage during the neighborhood's development work," the IAA said in a statement.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNEARTH SECRET CHURCH TIED TO COUNCIL OF NICAEA, CHRISTIANITY'S DEFINING MOMENT

"When construction is completed, the mikveh will be returned to the site, and integrated into an open public space that will stand at the heart of the new neighborhood."

The discovery helps bring the biblical world to life, according to Dinesh D'Souza, an author, commentator and Christian apologist who spoke to Fox News Digital about the find.

"It’s quite remarkable because I’ve seen these ritual baths, these mikveh[s]," D'Souza said.

"They’re usually pretty small."

He added, "It gives you a vivid picture. In some ways, it brings the Bible to life, both the Old Testament and the New, because this mikveh reflects the times right around the time of Jesus."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

He added, "This is confirming, describing, illuminating the world of the Bible. That’s one of the things that biblical archaeology can do. It can authenticate the historicity of the Bible — not the theology, not the miracles, but the historicity of it."

D’Souza's new book, "The Stones Cry Out," as well as his documentary of the same name, were the result of extensive research into biblical archaeology. He pointed to the Pool of Siloam as a significant example of an ancient ritual bath with biblical connections.

"The Pool of Siloam connects to the temple by the Pilgrimage Road, a road on which almost certainly Jesus walked," D'Souza said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"For me as a believer, it is chilling to sort of stand in these locations, observe them, walk the Pilgrimage Road, because in a sense you are connecting in a very experiential way with these profound artifacts of ancient times."

D'Souza said he sees a broader significance in biblical archaeology beyond what such discoveries reveal about ancient Israel.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Western civilization and America are based on the sort of anchors or twin pillars of Athens and Jerusalem," he said. "To me, the archaeology of Jerusalem is supporting that Jerusalem pillar of Athens and Jerusalem."

"In other words, there is a relevance not just to Israel, but to Western civilization as a whole and specifically to America."

item.title: Wynonna Judd admits helping daughter during meth battle ‘bit me in the butt'
item.description: Wynonna Judd reveals she enabled Grace Kelley's meth addiction by giving her money for drugs, a painful realization explored on her album "The Hard Truth."
item.content:encoded:
Wynonna Judd is reflecting on the painful lesson she learned while trying to help her daughter Grace Kelley through her years-long battle with methamphetamine addiction.

Kelley, 30, has struggled with drug addiction and faced a string of related legal troubles for more than a decade. She is currently serving a 15-month sentence at Rockingham County Jail in Harrisonburg, Virginia, after pleading guilty in June to a felony charge of driving with a suspended or revoked license.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, Judd, 62, who recently released her deeply personal album "The Hard Truth," candidly opened up about coming to the realization that some of her attempts to help Kelley only exacerbated her daughter's problems.

CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT

"I really lost myself with Grace and I enabled her, which comes down to basically giving her money for drugs," Judd admitted. "And here I thought I was buying her a car. And those things really bit me in the butt."

"And I'm still feeling, you know, some guilt and shame about that," she added.

LADY A'S CHARLES KELLEY SHARES BEFORE-AND-AFTER PHOTOS SHOWING HOW SOBRIETY TRANSFORMED HIS LIFE

The country star also shared what she would tell other parents struggling to help their children without enabling them.

"I would say work on yourself," Judd said. "That was one of the things that I was told. And working on myself, getting the peace, letting her see that she's attracted to that. Maybe she wants to get better herself. So let the light shine."

COUNTRY HITMAKER REVEALS HOW FAITH CARRIED HIM THROUGH SON'S MURDER — AND TOWARD COMPASSION FOR HIS KILLER

"Let your light shine through the cracks, that's how they see the light," she continued. "And hopefully she'll want the same thing that I have. Find someone whose recovery you love so much that you want to be like them and go and do it."

"The Hard Truth" is Judd's first solo studio album in more than a decade as well as her first time serving as a primary songwriter. The album explores heartbreak, healing, faith and survival while shining a light on some of the most painful chapters of Judd's life, including her complicated relationship with her late mother Naomi Judd and Kelley's struggles.

WATCH: WYNONNA JUDD SAYS HELPING DAUGHTER THROUGH METH BATTLE ‘BIT ME IN THE BUTT’

HAYDEN PANETTIERE DEFENDS GIVING UP CUSTODY OF HER DAUGHTER DESPITE INTENSE 'EMOTIONAL PAIN'

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Judd opened up about the hardest truth that she had to face while making the album.

"That there might be a chance that my daughter doesn't get clean, that she doesn't find the healing that she so desperately needs," Judd admitted. "As a mother, I'm devastated by her story, and I just had to let go."

‘NO CONTACT’ ON THE RISE: NEARLY 2 IN 5 AMERICANS CUT TIES WITH LOVED ONES

The six-time Grammy Award winner also reflected on her current estrangement from Kelley, with whom she said she has not spoken for a year.

"After all these years, the money ran out, and she did, too," Judd said. "And I just have to make peace with the fact that I did everything I could do. Including enabling, and I've had to deal with that. And just the pain of losing her to meth and realizing that there's absolutely nothing I can do to save her anymore."

'BAYWATCH: HAWAII' STAR BRANDY LEDFORD SAYS SHE 'WANTED TO TRULY CHECK OUT' BEFORE REHAB SAVED HER LIFE

Judd explained that her last conversation with Kelley was difficult since she had stood by her decision to stop enabling her daughter.

"Things were tense because I wasn't giving her money anymore and helping her to go back to rehab again and again and again, and again," Judd said. "And I just had to say, 'Sweetheart, you know, you're 30 years old. It's time to stop blaming your mom. And I want you to get the help that you need, and you're gonna have to do it yourself.'"

COUNTRY SINGER RUSTON KELLY COMMITS TO SOBRIETY AFTER RELAPSING ON DRUGS FOLLOWING FREAK GOLF CART CRASH

Judd told Fox News Digital that while she still has hope for a reconciliation with Kelley, there is one condition that would have to come first before they could begin rebuilding their relationship.

"Sobriety," she said. "You are not supposed to make any major decisions in your life, including relationships for a year after you get clean and sober. And I would ask her to go to rehab again, because I know that that's what worked for me."

CARA DELEVINGNE ADMITS SHE USED PARTY DRUG GHB DAILY BEFORE TERRIFYING SEIZURES FORCED HER SOBER

In 2006, Judd checked herself into the Shades of Hope Center of Headling in Buffalo Gap, Texas, where she underwent a 42-day treatment program to address her struggles with food addiction. She told Fox News Digital that her own time in treatment shaped the way she views recovery and the example she wants to set for Kelley.

"I'm gonna express that to her, of course, and you're not supposed to really go there. You want the person to want it themselves," Judd said. "But it would take some time because we've been apart a lot. She's been homeless and struggling for years and in and out of prison."

"And I have a song on the record called ‘Drive,’ which talks about me driving down to see her in prison back when she was incarcerated," she continued. "And I'm just gonna look forward to that day. I still have hope she's alive. There is still hope."

Judd shares Kelley and son Elijah, 31, with her first husband Arch Kelley III, to whom she was married from 1996 to 1998.

During a recent appearance on the "Shawn Ryan Show," Judd reflected on how her demanding career may have affected Grace differently than it did Elijah.

"Grace was very jealous of my career because it took me away from her enough to where she was not satisfied," she said. "I think because she's the second born, I think it was important to her that I even spend more time with her because I had that with Elijah for a minute."

"He was more at peace about it," Judd continued. "She was the one that wanted to sleep with me, wanted my attention 24/7."

"So that was painful. That was hard. I was really hard on myself about that," she admitted.

Judd also spoke candidly about the toll of her daughter’s addiction, describing herself as "a mom in waiting."

"I'm waiting for my daughter to return from a nightmarish addiction to meth," she said. "And it has been quite a journey."

"And unfortunately, she's been incarcerated since … on and off since she was 17," she continued.

"I've made all the jokes about, 'I have one on parole. I have one on patrol,'" Judd added. "My son is a deputy. I've done all that, and now it's time to just tell my story as a mom who's constantly in this place between hell and hallelujah."

Judd said setting boundaries with Kelley became one of the hardest decisions of her life, recalling how she struggled with refusing to help her daughter even when she reached out in desperation.

"I had to let go, and that means no more enabling," she explained. "And it about killed me because when your kid calls and says, 'I'm hungry,' what do you do?"

The "No One Else on Earth" singer said Kelley’s repeated incarceration and the dangers surrounding drug use made her realize that enabling her daughter could have life-or-death consequences.

"She's been in and out of prison and jail for so long that that's her way of walking through the addiction part in terms of what it costs her," Judd said. "We're also now dealing with fentanyl. So, there's that."

"I realized, 'Oh my God, it's possible that I could be part of the reason she dies. I'm loving her to death. Literally,'" she shared.

Judd said she believes that Kelley still carries resentment over the time her career took away from their relationship, as well as her decision to step in and raise her granddaughter Kaliyah.

"Grace is really mad at me right now," she said. "Because I had a career, and I was busy, and she didn't have enough of me in the beginning. I did the best I could. I've made a lot of mistakes, and she's really mad at me for stepping in with her child."

"Kaliyah has Type 1 diabetes," Judd continued. "There's no way she could have taken care of her. That's one thing. It's a 24/7 situation. I stepped in, and I took over, and she's mad at me."

"I understand that that's her journey," she added. "It's not mine. My journey is to raise this baby to be the healthiest and break the cycle."

Judd and her third husband, musician Cactus Moser, who she married in 2012, have been the primary caregivers for Kaliyah, 4, since her infancy and legally adopted her amid Kelley's addiction struggles and legal woes. The singer was previously married to former bodyguard D.R. Roach from 2003 until 2007.

Moser and Judd are currently raising Kaliyah on their 500-acre farm in Tennessee.

When asked by Fox News Digital about how she balances protecting Kaliyah while leaving the door open for Kelley to be part of her life someday, Judd said her focus remains on giving her granddaughter a grounded childhood.

"I haven't answered that yet," she said. "I think I'm still in the part where I'm so hell-bent on keeping her out of the iPad and the phone and TV. We live on a farm, and she mucks stalls and does chores and she's a cowgirl. So I'm so centered on that. I haven't really given that a lot of thought and if and when that happens I'll answer your question."

Judd also shared a glimpse into her day-to-day life on the farm with Kaliyah and Moser.

"Getting away with as much as possible without having to do anything, going on a side by side, ride down to the lake, taking her fishing, we do that a lot," she told Fox News Digital. "And being out in the woods, just being outside is just so heavenly."

Judd described their farm as a "peace place," noting that her life at home is much simpler than her life onstage.

"I have 40 animals," she said. "So I have chores as well. And I spend my time cooking. That's what I do."

"I'm known in our family as the cook, and I'm known as Nonie," Judd continued. "When I don't have on my lashes, I am known as Nonie."

Meanwhile, Kelley is believed to have welcomed a second child while incarcerated. During her appearance on the "Shawn Ryan Show," Judd said she learned about the baby through social media and knows little about the child’s circumstances.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I just found out on TikTok that she's had another baby in prison, and I don't even know if it's a boy or a girl," Judd said.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"There are these things that people assume that I can do, but I'm just a mom in this situation," she continued. "Sure, I can get a good seat in a restaurant. I can stand on the mountaintops and sing from my toenails, but this one thing I have no control."

"It's just one of those nightmarish things that you hope you wake up from," Judd added.

item.title: Washington jewelry store owner opens fire after would-be thieves ram truck through storefront
item.description: Surveillance video shows a Toyota Tacoma smashing through a Lynnwood jewelry store before masked suspects rush in carrying an axe in broad daylight.
item.content:encoded:
Masked would-be thieves smashed a pickup truck through the front of a Washington jewelry store in broad daylight and stormed inside — only to be sent scrambling when the store owner pulled a gun and opened fire, according to authorities and a local report.

The attempted robbery unfolded shortly after 12:25 p.m. on Tuesday at Medina Jewelers in Lynnwood.

Surveillance video shows three vehicles circling the parking lot before a white Toyota Tacoma barrels through the storefront, shattering glass and sending employees running.

WATCH: MASKED THIEVES WIELDING HAMMERS HIT JEWELRY STORE IN WHAT EXPERT CALLS 'MOB-STYLE' HEIST

Several masked suspects then rush through the opening, including one who appears to be carrying an axe.

The store owner grabbed a gun and fired, sending the group fleeing empty-handed, according to FOX13 Seattle.

No injuries were reported at the scene, though police said it was unclear whether any of the suspects had been struck by gunfire.

REPEAT OFFENDER BUSTED AGAIN LESS THAN 24 HOURS AFTER RELEASE IN BRAZEN JEWELRY STORE THEFT CASE: POLICE

"It was broad daylight and a pretty rare occurrence for us," Lynnwood Police Cmdr. Joe Dickenson told the outlet.

Police were still working to determine whether any of the suspects had a firearm.

"You had several witnesses that were out and about, several pedestrians walking around; all of a sudden, a car crashing into a building and shots ringing out is cause for alarm," Dickenson said.

The suspects escaped in a black BMW SUV and a silver Toyota or Infiniti sedan, police said. The BMW struck a parked vehicle while fleeing and may have damage to its front passenger side.

Detectives are asking anyone who recognizes the suspects or vehicles captured on surveillance footage to send tips to crimetips@lynnwoodwa.gov and reference case No. 2026-37986.

item.title: Sarah Spain calls Fever GM 'defensive' for defending fans, but has plenty to say to her own critics
item.description: Sarah Spain assumed Indiana Fever fans had been ejected from WNBA games, but GM Amber Cox's security records challenged that entire narrative.
item.content:encoded:
Sarah Spain thought Indiana Fever fans had been removed from games for violating the WNBA's fan code of conduct. Then general manager Amber Cox said no fans had been removed from the team's home games this season, citing the organization's security records.

That news surprised Spain ... but it didn't stop her from criticizing Cox for sounding "defensive" in her rebuttal.

Well, wouldn't you be defensive if people kept trashing your fans and you had information that contradicted what they were saying?

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Spain certainly understands wanting to defend herself. When she didn't like one of my columns, she devoted part of her podcast to complaining about it.

But when Cox pushes back on the media, Spain has a problem with her tone.

"The attacks on our fan base have no basis in reality, and they need to stop, especially with members of the media," Cox said during her season-ending news conference. She clarified that she was referring to media who hadn't attended a game at Gainbridge Fieldhouse.

LEFT-WING SPORTS HOST SARAH SPAIN LAUNCHES DISGUSTING PERSONAL SMEAR OF SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM

Cox acknowledged that bad behavior happens and said anyone crossing the line, online or in an arena, should be held accountable. But she also had information about the fans actually attending her team's games.

"We did not have one fan pointed out by a player who violated the WNBA code of conduct this season. Not one fan was removed from a game," Cox said. "We take this really seriously, and that is backed up by our security stats and the lived experiences of countless fans who we host at every game."

"To be characterized in such a broad stroke is not fair," she added.

On a recent episode of her podcast, Spain credited Cox for providing that information. Perhaps more telling, though, is what Spain had assumed before hearing Cox's comments:

"I thought that there had been at least one incident where fans were removed and it had been clear that there had been an incident," Spain said.

Which incident? What did the fan do? Where did she get that impression? Spain didn't identify the incident she had in mind or where she had heard about it, leaving listeners unable to check it against Cox's statement.

Instead, Spain argued that Cox needed to acknowledge why players and visiting fans might feel there was a problem. So, even after presenting information that challenged the accusations against her fans, Cox still owed the people making those accusations a more accommodating response, according to Spain.

Later, while agreeing with guest Jordan Robinson's criticism, Spain said: "The defensiveness as opposed to the openness. Not we want to fix why people have the wrong idea. Instead, people have the wrong idea and we're mad at them."

Yes, Sarah. People can have the wrong idea, and the people they're talking about can be mad about it. Especially when those people have been repeatedly called racists and bigots.

Cox had already called for accountability for actual misconduct and cited the team's security records to defend her fans. Spain still wanted her to be more accommodating, but Cox's job isn't to make the people trashing her fans feel better about being challenged.

There's a bit of a Mandela Effect going on with the left-wing media and Fever fans. Allegations get remembered as proven misconduct, and fans who chose to leave get remembered as having been kicked out.

In May 2025, the WNBA investigated allegations of racist fan behavior during a Fever-Sky game. The league reviewed audio and video and gathered information from fans, team personnel and arena staff. The WNBA concluded that it could "not substantiate" the allegations.

I wrote about ESPN's coverage while that investigation was still underway because commentators were plowing ahead with the narrative that Fever fans are racist without waiting for any evidence.

ESPN’S FAVORITE INSIDER ACCIDENTALLY EXPLAINED WHY MOST AMERICANS DON’T TRUST THE MEDIA

This year, in August, Las Vegas Aces guard Jackie Young complained about a Fever fan during a game, and security pulled him aside. The fan voluntarily chose to leave and the Fever later explained that security found no code-of-conduct violation and hadn't ejected him.

But by then, media have already described the encounter as an ejection. People who missed the Fever's explanation were getting the wrong account of what happened.

Then there was A'ja Wilson's confrontation with a Fever fan during last week's playoff game. The Fever said security spoke with the fan and witnesses, found no code-of-conduct violation and didn't remove the fan from the arena.

Spain did distinguish that encounter from other incidents involving alleged racist rhetoric and also said individual encounters should be assessed separately. OK, then apply that to the broader accusations against Fever fans. Which incidents support them, and which have been repeated so often that people just assume they happened?

Online trolls posting hateful comments on social media don't establish how the crowd at Gainbridge behaves. Nor does a player confronting or complaining about a fan establish that the fan crossed the line. Yet, the media loves to immediately rush to the defense of these WNBA players without evidence.

Spain was surprised by Cox's account of the team's security record. I'd have liked to hear more about why she had a different impression and less about whether Cox sounded sufficiently open-minded while correcting it.

My suspicion is that she gets her news almost exclusively from left-wing outlets, so she hears plenty about the accusations against Fever fans and a lot less about the reporting that challenges them.

For what it's worth, Spain says she doesn't use X anymore, opting instead to post and read posts on Bluesky. Do with that information what you will.

In August, I argued that Spain's preferred approach to WNBA media sounded more like public relations than journalism. My commentary was based entirely on her own words, not something I invented out of thin air.

Spain wasn't pleased.

On her Sept. 16 show, she referred to "my own former colleague who now works at that outlet" before discussing coverage of her comments about WNBA media credentials. That was me. We both worked at ESPN, the outlet she was talking about is OutKick and the column she described was mine.

"They reworded that as me saying real media, which is just PR for the players," she complained. Then she accused the outlet of "asking the same question 8,000 times in order to keep doing the same story over and over for clicks."

Careful, Sarah, because that sounds awfully defensive to me. You should show more openness and ask why I had those thoughts rather than getting mad that I had them. Am I doing this right?

FORMER ESPN RADIO HOST SARAH SPAIN REFERRED TO J.D. VANCE AS A 'DEMON' AND 'THE DEVIL'

And that Sept. 16 episode had another example of Spain finding plenty of room for nuance when the subject was Sarah Spain. While criticizing Sydney Sweeney's Novig ad, she recalled starting her own on-camera career in cut-up jerseys and push-up bras.

Her response to people using those pictures against her?

"Hate the game, not the player."

But we're not done. She also defended her "publicity stunt" to get Super Bowl tickets. In 2007, Spain posted an eBay ad offering to be someone's date to the game, complete with a photo of herself in a Chicago Bears cheerleader costume, cleavage on full display.

Spain called it "this really clever viral idea that ended up getting me tickets to the game and all these connections." She was "using the system," she explained, and later used those contacts to get jobs.

So, Spain's defense was that women trying to break into sports faced fewer opportunities then and she basically had no choice but to try and use sex appeal to further her career.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

But, when discussing Sweeney, Spain complained that "we're back to this bulls--t where if a woman is involved in speaking to men, she should be naked."

I'd have more patience for that lecture if she extended Sweeney a little of the generosity she demands when discussing her own career. And I'd have more patience for her criticism of Cox if she hadn't demonstrated, at length, how much she values the chance to defend herself.

Spain was still talking about her critics in a more recent episode, during a conversation with influencer Coach Jackie. She described outlets as "so obsessed with what I'm doing" and said: "Like, the people who suck, I don't care how many stories they write about me, but I don't want to let the story get bigger because of it."

She's certainly keeping up with the coverage. She knew enough about my column to dispute its argument on her show. That's fine, but it makes her reaction to Cox harder to take seriously. She knows exactly why someone might want to challenge a story about them, especially if they believe the story is unfair or unfounded (though my column was neither).

Spain has talked about letting "garbage content" die in darkness. I take the opposite view: sunlight is the best disinfectant. If she makes a bad argument about Fever fans, I'm going to write about it. Her deciding that the people criticizing her radical opinions "suck" isn't much of a rebuttal.

During that same interview, while discussing pressure to comment on controversies, she also said, "I hate disappointing people I agree with."

Cox gave Spain a reason to revisit what she believed about Fever fans. Spain acknowledged the information, then got back to criticizing the Fever's response. I'd like to know what, if anything, would make her reconsider the coverage instead.

If Spain is worried about disappointing people who share her views, how willing is she to tell them something they don't want to hear?

item.title: House Republican warns CBDC 'communist money' could lead US to 'dystopian' future
item.description: Republican Rep. Warren Davidson of Ohio plans to introduce legislation that seeks to prevent the creation of a central bank digital currency.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio, plans to introduce legislation that puts the prospect of a central bank digital currency (CBDC) in the crosshairs.

The lawmaker, who has served in the U.S. House since mid-2016 and is currently seeking re-election, characterized central bank digital currency as "communist money for the digital age," during an interview with Fox News Digital.

"They could just freeze your money. You could program it. Some people call it a feature," Davidson said. He provided a scenario in which a pickup truck driver pays $10 per gallon for fuel while a hybrid driver could get their fuel for just $2 per gallon. "And people see this as a feature. I think it's dystopian," Davidson said, adding, "I definitely want to stop it."

Last month, in a post on X, Davidson wrote, "I'm drafting a bill to regulate Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) as counterfeit money. Planning a CBDC? Conspiracy. Designing a CBDC? Same as designing counterfeit plates. Launching CBDC? Counterfeiting. Prison for counterfeiters and their accomplices. No CBDC!"

TRUMP TAKES UNUSUAL STEP, LETS BIPARTISAN HOUSING BILL BECOME LAW UNSIGNED AMID SAVE PRESSURE CAMPAIGN

In another post on X last month, Davidson warned, "CBDC = communist money for the digital age. Programmable money puts the government between you and your money. You will only have access with their permission. This is an existential threat to western civilization."

While a section within the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act that became law earlier this year temporarily prohibits the creation of a CBDC, that ban sunsets in a few years — language in the ban notes that "provisions of this section shall cease to be effective on December 31, 2030."

Davidson told Fox News Digital during the interview on Tuesday that "the fundamentals for sound money is some level of fiscal discipline," adding that "you can't spend more than you bring in every year."

"I don't think it has to be gold," he said, explaining that there needs to be "a disciplined monetary policy" in which "you can't grow the money supply disproportionate to your economy."

HOUSE REPUBLICAN SUGGESTS SEN DARLINE GRAHAM IS AN 'ALLY' FOR THE 'SWAMP'

"I think we should end this Fed," Davidson said, adding that he believes there is "a case for a central bank," while noting, "I don't know that you could reform the current one without ending it."

Davidson said that he thinks "we should at least audit the Fed."

Asked about President Donald Trump's proposal to dole out $5,000 to every American adult if the GOP wins both chambers of Congress during the midterms, Davidson indicated that he could get behind the policy if it is paired with spending cuts to cover the cost.

GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US'

Davidson said that "on its face" the proposal is concerning "because $5,000 per person going into the economy would fuel inflation," but suggested that such a move could be combined with action such as gutting Obamacare, saying that among "the most promising ways to pay for it is a radical shift in healthcare."

item.title: Doctor reveals 4 hidden health risks of spending too much time indoors
item.description: A Nature & Health Alliance survey finds nearly half of Americans spend under two hours outdoors weekly, fueling burnout, brain fog and belly fat.
item.content:encoded:
Nearly half of Americans spend less than two hours outdoors in an entire week, according to a new national survey from the Nature & Health Alliance involving researchers at Texas A&M University.

Dr. John La Puma, a California physician and expert in nature-based medicine, has focused on the potential health impacts of spending less time outdoors.

In his book, "Indoor Epidemic," he discusses how humans spend about 93% of their lives inside, which comes with a "hidden health tax." He claims the remedy is a simple 7% outdoor prescription.

NEARLY 3 IN 4 AMERICANS ARE BATTLING THE SAME EXHAUSTING HEALTH PROBLEM, CDC REVEALS

"Many people don't realize that they're inhibited from feeling as good as they can, because they're exhausted even after a full night's sleep," La Puma told Fox News Digital. "They need coffee to feel normal. They crash at 2 in the afternoon. They're wired at night. They can't go to sleep, but their labs are normal."

"And they come into the office saying, ‘Why do I feel so exhausted?’ It's the four Bs," he said.

Outdoor light can be many times brighter than typical indoor lighting, La Puma noted, making it a powerful signal for setting the body’s internal clock, or circadian rhythm.

"If you don't set your body clock, your body doesn't know what time it is, and it just goes to sleep whenever you can get to sleep instead of on time," he told Fox News Digital.

SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISINGLY EASY EXERCISE THAT MAY BOOST YOUR MOOD IN JUST 10 MINUTES

Getting bright outdoor light soon after waking can help synchronize the body's sleep-wake cycle and support the natural rise in melatonin later in the evening, according to La Puma.

He recommends spending about 10 minutes outdoors within the first hour of waking, without sunglasses.

La Puma uses the term "ultraprocessed time" to describe hours lost to screens, scrolling and other digital distractions.

"Ultraprocessed time is kind of like ultraprocessed food," he said. "It’s not nutritious. It’s synthetic. It’s artificial. It’s ubiquitous."

That includes time spent endlessly scrolling, he said, which can seem to simply "evaporate."

La Puma argues that a person’s environment can contribute to burnout, rather than viewing it solely as a matter of willpower.

AMERICA'S NATIONAL PARKS COULD ADD YEARS TO YOUR LIFE — HERE'S HOW THEY BOOST HEALTH

Spending excessive time indoors can lead to an overload of screen exposure, he said, as people often turn to the same devices for work, entertainment and relaxation. He noted that the body may not interpret screen time as true rest or escape.

"And equally important, no horizon. We are horizon-deprived as a species because indoors, we can't see more than 20 feet in front of us," La Puma said.

To combat burnout, he recommends getting up and going to the window and looking outside for a minute every hour.

"It relaxes your eyes, relaxes the muscles around your temples, reduces headache if you have it, improves energy and reduces fatigue," he said. "That's the beginning of being able to reverse burnout."

DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE

Simply going outside during the workday can help to reverse burnout, LaPuma said.

"Your eyes need distance like your lungs need air."

People who spend the day indoors may notice that they feel mentally foggy by the afternoon, La Puma said, particularly in poorly ventilated spaces where carbon dioxide can build up.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Indoor CO₂ levels can climb above 1,000 parts per million in poorly ventilated spaces, and some research has linked elevated levels with reduced cognitive performance.

"So it's not that you're just making bad decisions in the afternoons — there's a biologic reason for it," La Puma said.

"What you need to do is cross-ventilate, but that's tough to do in an office or conference room."

The doctor said that getting outdoors gives the eyes a chance to focus at greater distances while providing a break from potentially stuffy indoor air. The EPA notes that concentrations of some pollutants can be two to five times higher indoors than outdoors.

When someone’s body clock is out of sync, it can disrupt the body’s normal cortisol rhythm, La Puma said.

Cortisol, often called the stress hormone, naturally rises and falls throughout the day. Research has linked altered cortisol activity with greater abdominal and visceral fat, although the relationship is complex.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Again, the way to improve your metabolism is to get daylight at the right time, in the right place, for the right duration — early in the morning especially," La Puma advised.

"This will give you a bump in cortisol, which you want early in the morning to feel awake, and then it drops appropriately."

Most people spend about an hour outdoors each day as they walk from the car to the office, for example — but that's what La Puma calls "incidental time," not "biologically active time."

To combat the four Bs, he recommends spending "intentional time" outdoors, "in a blue or green space," for a minimum effective dose of 17 minutes a day.

"Be intentional with your time — look at the sky in the morning … to reset your body clock and watch the clouds," the doctor advised.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For those who live in a big city and can’t see the sky, La Puma recommends looking at a distant rooftop, or looking through an open window when going outside isn’t possible. The goal is to focus beyond the confines of an indoor space.

"So 17 minutes a day is the minimum effective dose — that's all it takes to begin to bend the curve on the four Bs," he said.

"You can turn those minutes into medicine."

item.title: AI in education gives us a chance to use the best tech to fix our broken schools
item.description: Artificial intelligence in education offers a rare chance to avoid social media's mistakes by establishing child safety safeguards before harm occurs.
item.content:encoded:
The lesson of social media is not that transformative technologies should be feared. It is that when children are involved, safeguards must come before harm — not after.

For years, social media platforms expanded with few meaningful protections for child safety, transparency, age-appropriate design, parental visibility or independent oversight. Only after mounting evidence of harm did policymakers begin responding in earnest. By then, millions of children had already been shaped by systems designed to maximize engagement.

Artificial intelligence (AI) gives us a rare chance to do better.

UK TO BAN TIKTOK, YOUTUBE, OTHER SOCIAL MEDIA APPS FOR CHILDREN UNDER 16, STARMER SAYS

AI has extraordinary potential in education. It can personalize support, extend teacher capacity, widen access and help students learn in new ways. But it can also shape how children think, write, reason and engage with the world. That is why this moment matters. Unlike social media, AI arrives with the benefit of hindsight. We already know what happens when powerful technologies become deeply embedded in the lives of children before society establishes clear rules for safety, accountability and transparency.

We should not make the same mistake twice.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: LAWMAKERS WRESTLE OVER WHETHER AI CAN MAKE THE GRADE IN AMERICA'S CLASSROOMS

A responsible framework for AI in education should begin with a simple principle: artificial intelligence must enhance human learning, not replace humans or their judgment.

Teachers must remain in charge of instruction, grading and curriculum. Parents must remain the primary decision-makers in their children’s education, with meaningful visibility into how AI interacts with their child, what information it collects and how recommendations are generated. And students must continue developing the habits that define real learning: reasoning, writing, discernment, persistence and critical thought.

WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI CAN MIMIC A TEACHER, BUT IT CANNOT SHEPHERD A SOUL

That is also why this conversation must be about more than artificial intelligence alone. It must also be about Ethical Intelligence.

AI can make learning faster, more personalized and more efficient. Ethical Intelligence ensures it remains human. It asks the questions technology cannot answer on its own: What is true? What is good? What is fair? What does responsibility require? What kind of person is this tool helping a child become?

WHEN AI TESTS CAUSE DAMAGE, WE NEED STRONGER SAFEGUARDS AND REAL ACCOUNTABILITY

That distinction is essential. Intelligence without ethics can optimize for convenience while weakening formation. It can deliver answers without judgment, speed without wisdom and personalization without character. In education, that is not progress.

That means student-facing AI should meet clear standards before it is widely deployed. Those standards should include transparency about where and how AI is used; strong protections for student privacy; limits on data collection and commercialization; preservation of teacher authority over grading and instruction; prohibitions on manipulation, behavioral profiling and hidden influence; age-appropriate outputs and meaningful parental notice, access and oversight.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

Just as important, educational AI should demonstrate both safety and effectiveness before it reaches millions of children. Classroom-based pilot testing should be the norm, not the exception. "Deploy first and regulate later" was the defining mistake of the social media era. Education cannot afford to repeat it.

The deepest safeguard, however, is philosophical, not technical.

CHRISTIAN UNIVERSITY AIMS TO PRODUCE 'IRREPLACEABLE' GRADUATES AS AI RESHAPES HIGHER EDUCATION

Artificial intelligence should function as a tutor, coach, research assistant and productivity tool — not as a substitute for the intellectual and moral development of children. Education is not simply about getting answers. It is about learning how to think, how to judge, how to wrestle with complexity and how to grow in both knowledge and character. Resilience, wisdom, creativity and conviction are formed through effort, reflection and struggle. AI can support that process. It should never short-circuit it.

Every transformative technology brings both promise and risk. The internet expanded access to knowledge while introducing new vulnerabilities. Social media connected billions of people while contributing to serious harms, especially for young users. AI may become one of the most beneficial innovations in the history of education — but only if it is governed by a framework that protects children while preserving the true purpose of schooling.

WHAT META'S NEW TEEN RESTRICTIONS MEAN FOR YOUNG PEOPLE

This is the rare opportunity now before policymakers.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

For the first time in the digital age, leaders can establish meaningful safeguards before a transformative technology becomes fully embedded in the daily lives of children. By insisting on transparency, parental rights, teacher authority, student privacy, age-appropriate design, independent testing and educational accountability, states can encourage innovation while making clear that technology must serve education — not the other way around.

Social media showed what happens when innovation outpaces responsibility. AI presents a rare opportunity to reverse that lesson. Before artificial intelligence reshapes childhood, we must ensure that Ethical Intelligence shapes artificial intelligence. The future of education, and the character of the next generation, depends on it.

Ed Pozzuoli is an expert in education law and CEO of Tripp Scott Law Firm.

item.title: White Sox anger fans with lame first pitch pick for ALDS Game 3 after writers tease huge name
item.description: Chicago White Sox fans expected Barack Obama, Michael Jordan, or even Pope Leo XIV for the first pitch, but instead got a mostly unknown actor.
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago White Sox are suddenly the talk of the Second City. 

After years, decades even, of futility, the South Siders finally have the type of young, exciting team that fans love. And even better, they're a good, young, exciting team.

Chicago took a quick 2-0 series lead over their division rivals, the Cleveland Guardians, winning both games on the road and setting up a huge game three back at Rate Field. A huge game three not just because the White Sox had an opportunity to clinch an ALCS appearance, but for the opportunity to do it at home.

As hard as it is to believe, a win in game three would be the first clincher in front of home White Sox fans since ... 1906. Three years after the first flight. A year before the first color photograph. And two years before Ford rolled out the first ever Model T.

WHITE SOX RIDE ANOTHER DRAMATIC COMEBACK WIN TO BEAT GUARDIANS AND TAKE COMMANDING 2-0 ALDS LEAD

And the fans were ready. Rate Field was packed for first pitch, with a jubilant, electric atmosphere, something that seemed virtually impossible just two years ago.

They were even more excited when online speculation started that there'd be a big Chicago name heading to the mound for the ceremonial first pitch. Some thought former President Barack Obama, maybe Michael Jordan, who of course played with the White Sox, Derrick Rose, or even the team's most famous fan: Pope Leo XIV.

MLB.com's Scott Merkin sent the anticipation to a fever pitch when he posted on X that there would be a "big name" heading to the mound. "No hints given, so have at it," he said.

Just imagine, taking your young kid to the biggest home White Sox playoff game of his life, literally, and telling him to expect to see a huge local figure there too. The Pope? Michael Jordan? A former president? Some other Chicago legend? A popular White Sox player?

That anticipation, after spending a fortune on playoff tickets and fighting through traffic and stadium security to get to the building and it's ... Belmont Cameli.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Quick, try to figure out who Belmont Cameli is without looking it up.

Well, we looked it up, and yeah, we're still not sure what they were thinking. Cameli is apparently an actor most known for portraying a hockey player in an Amazon series, "Off Campus."

Maybe Merkin said that he wouldn't give any hints because he had no idea who Belmont Cameli was.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

To be fair to the White Sox, he is from nearby Naperville, Ill., so there's some local connection there. It's also a massive letdown to go into a game expecting a big name and getting a mostly unknown actor. One user on X posted a common criticism.

"Are you telling me Sox fans thought the Pope of the one, holy, catholic, and apostolic Church was throwing out the first pitch today and it was just a guy from one of the horny hockey shows?" the post said.

To his credit, at least Cameli gave it his all.

The frenzied White Sox home crowd got over the disappointment quickly, as they jumped out to a 1-0 lead in the first inning. But the Guardians roared back, scoring nine runs and keeping Chicago's powerful offense at bay. The day started with a big letdown and ended with a 9-3 loss to set up game four.

But hey, the good news for White Sox fans is that the team has another opportunity to bring out a complete nobody to throw the first pitch for game four on Thursday night.
